d: Meshes are a collection of vertices, edges, and faces that make up 3D objects.
h:
MeshPart objects are descendants of the BasePart class. They represent meshes, which are collections of vertices, edges, and faces that make up a 3D object. Unlike parts, which you can directly create in Studio, you need to use a third-party modeling application like Blender or Maya to create meshes, then import them into Studio as MeshPart objects.

After importing a mesh into Studio, you can customize its rendering properties, such as textures, level of detail, and collision fidelity. In addition to importing your own meshes, you can also browse and select from user-uploaded meshes using the Creator Store.

Roblox supports many types of meshes, as long as they adhere to the general mesh specifications. A basic mesh consists of at least one mesh object and one texture:

Studio also supports meshes with components for creating avatar character models or accessories, such as rigging and skinning data.

You can sell MeshPart assets as avatar bodies, accessories, and clothing on the Marketplace. See Avatar for more information.

Import meshes

You can import meshes into Studio using the Importer. With this tool, you can preview and examine meshes before importing them into your workspace or Toolbox, such as verifying texture, rigging, skinning, and animation data. It also flags issues and rejects meshes with error.

If the mesh file you are importing contains objects using specific naming conventions or contains facial animation data, the Importer automatically detects and converts them into the following objects instead of MeshPart:

  • Attachment — Objects with _Att at the end of their names.
  • WrapTarget — Objects with _OuterCage at the end of their names.
  • WrapLayer — Objects with both _InnerCage _OuterCage at the end of their names.
  • FaceControls — Objects containing avatar character heads and the appropriate facial animation data.

If you want to bulk-import meshes along with non-3D assets, such as images and audio, you can use the Asset Manager; note, however, that it doesn't support importing meshes with rigging, skinning, and animation data, accessories, or characters with facial animations.

Customize meshes

Unlike basic parts, meshes have more customization options that you can adjust for advanced rendering fidelity.

Texture

Textures contribute to the visual appearance of meshes by adding 2D details such as color and patterns. Studio allows you to either apply one texture using the MeshPart.TextureID property, or apply up to four physically-based rendering (PBR) textures within a SurfaceAppearance child object of the mesh or made with a MaterialVariant and set in the mesh's MeshPart.MaterialVariant property. PBR textures allow you to represent realistic shading and lighting by using multiple types of texture images, or maps, on a single object.

Studio supports four PBR texture maps, each corresponding to a visual characteristic of an object's surface appearance. Combining multiple texture maps can more accurately simulate color, roughness, and reflectivity in any lighting environment, and enhance the visual elements of your assets and environment. For more information on PBR textures and the texture maps, see PBR Textures.

You can apply PBR textures using one of the following objects:

  • SurfaceAppearance — Applies PBR textures to the mesh surface and doesn't affect its geometry.
  • MaterialVariant — Represents a custom material that not only applies PBR textures to the mesh surface but also adds physical properties.

To add PBR textures to a mesh:

  1. In the Explorer window, hover over the MeshPart object. Click the ⊕ button and select SurfaceAppearance.
  2. In the Properties window, edit the properties corresponding to the PBR texture maps.
  1. In the Explorer window, hover over the MaterialService. Click the ⊕ button and select MaterialVariant.
  2. In the Properties window, edit the properties corresponding to the PBR texture maps.
  3. Name the new MaterialVariant to a name of your choice.
  4. Select the MeshPart and, in the Properties window, set the MaterialVariant to the one you just created.

If you both add SurfaceAppearance as a child object and set the MaterialVariant in the mesh's properties, Studio only applies the texture map settings of the SurfaceAppearance object to the mesh. The mesh still has all other settings of the MaterialVariant object, such as custom physical properties.

If the mesh you import to Studio doesn't come with texture data, or you want to change the existing texture, use the following steps to add a single texture:

  1. Import the texture file. The file must follow the texture specifications. Upon completion, Studio automatically assigns and prompts an asset ID.
  2. Copy the asset ID.
  3. In the Explorer window, select the MeshPart object.
  4. In the Properties window, select the TextureID field and paste the asset ID of the texture.

If your mesh has existing PBR textures, setting a Texture ID can't override the PBR textures.

Level of detail

You can dynamically control a mesh's level of detail using its RenderFidelity property. The default value is Automatic, meaning the mesh's detail is based on its distance from the camera as outlined in the following table.

Distance from camera Render fidelity Example
Less than 250 studs Highest
250-500 studs Medium
500 or more studs Lowest

Collision fidelity

Collision fidelity determines how closely the visual representation of a mesh matches its physical bounds. The MeshPart.CollisionFidelity property has the following options:

  • Box — Creates a bounding collision box, ideal for small or non‑interactive objects.
  • Hull — Generates a convex hull, suitable for objects with less pronounced indentations or cavities.
  • Default — Produces an approximate collision shape that supports concavity, suitable for complex objects with semi-detailed interaction needs.
  • PreciseConvexDecomposition — Offers the most precise fidelity but still not a 1:1 representation of the visual. This option has the most expensive performance cost and takes longer for the engine to compute.
  • Tunable — Setting MeshPart.CollisionFidelity to Tunable reveals a CollisionPrecision slider in the Properties window. Sliding up produces more precise, more expensive collision geometry, while sliding down produces coarser, cheaper geometry, all without switching to a different fidelity option. The default CollisionPrecision value isn't fixed; the engine intelligently picks the appropriate precision, and therefore cost, based on the size of the mesh.

To view collision fidelity in Studio, toggle on Collision fidelity from the Visualization Options widget in the upper‑right corner of the 3D viewport.

For more information on the performance impact of collision fidelity options and how to mitigate them, see Improve performance. For an in-depth walkthrough on how to choose a collision fidelity option that balances your precision and performance requirements, see Set physics and rendering parameters.

Rigging and skinning

Rigging is the process of connecting a mesh with an internal poseable skeleton rig. Rigged meshes allow mesh surfaces to rotate and move using internal bones within a model, such as a character's knee or elbow. Skinning a rigged mesh allows the rigged mesh object to deform, stretch, and bend in a more realistic manner.

For more information on rigging and skinning, see Rigging and skinning. After rigging a mesh, you can add animation and poses to it using the Animation Editor. See Create an animation for more information. Marketplace 3D assets, such as avatar clothing and bodies, also require rigging and skinning. See Avatar for more information on requirements for Marketplace assets.

kid.simple: A mesh is a detailed 3D shape, like a sword, a tree or a treasure chest, that you make in a 3D art program such as Blender and then bring into Studio as a MeshPart. Meshes can look far more detailed than anything built from basic parts. This page explains how to import meshes, paint them with textures, control how much detail shows at a distance, and pick how accurately they bump into things. Choosing the right settings keeps your game looking good and running fast.
kid.analogy: If basic parts are wooden building blocks, a mesh is a clay sculpture: you shape it in a separate workshop (Blender), then bring the finished sculpture into your room (Studio).
keyPoints: A MeshPart is a kind of part whose shape comes from a mesh made in another program, then brought in with the Importer.
The Importer lets you preview a mesh first and turns specially named objects into other things, for example names ending in `_Att` become Attachments.
You can paint a mesh with one image using `TextureID`, or with up to four realistic PBR maps using a SurfaceAppearance child or a MaterialVariant.
If a mesh has both a SurfaceAppearance and a MaterialVariant, the SurfaceAppearance's images win, but the MaterialVariant's physical settings still apply.
With `RenderFidelity` on Automatic, meshes show the most detail under 250 studs from the camera, medium detail from 250 to 500, and the lowest at 500 or more.
`CollisionFidelity` picks the invisible bump shape: Box (cheapest), Hull, Default, PreciseConvexDecomposition (most exact and most costly), or Tunable with a precision slider.
Turn on Collision fidelity in Visualization Options to see the invisible bump shapes.
Rigging adds a skeleton so a mesh can pose and animate, and skinning lets it bend smoothly, like a neck bending instead of the whole head swiveling.

terms.mesh: A 3D shape built from points (vertices), lines between them (edges) and flat surfaces (faces). A simple cube mesh has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces.
terms.MeshPart: A part that uses an imported mesh as its shape.
terms.import / Importer: Bringing a file from your computer into Studio. The Importer is the Studio window that does it and checks for problems.
terms.texture: A flat image wrapped around a 3D shape to give it color and patterns.
terms.PBR (physically based rendering): A way of drawing surfaces realistically by using several image maps, for example one for color, one for bumps, one for roughness and one for metal shine.
terms.texture map: One image that controls one look of the surface, like color or shininess.
terms.SurfaceAppearance: An object you put inside a MeshPart to give it PBR textures without changing how it behaves physically.
terms.MaterialVariant: A custom material with its own PBR textures and physical properties, kept in MaterialService.
terms.asset ID: The unique number Roblox gives an uploaded file, used to point to it, like `rbxassetid://123456`.
terms.level of detail / render fidelity: How detailed a mesh is drawn. Far-away meshes are drawn with fewer details to save effort. At 600 studs away, an Automatic mesh uses its lowest detail.
terms.collision fidelity: How closely the invisible bump shape matches the visible mesh. A donut with Box fidelity is solid in the middle, so you could not throw a ball through the hole.
terms.bounding box: The smallest box that fits all the way around the mesh.
terms.convex hull: The shape you would get by stretching plastic wrap tightly around the mesh. Dents and holes get filled in.
terms.concave / concavity: Having dents or hollows, like the inside of a bowl.
terms.rigging: Putting a skeleton of bones inside a mesh so parts of it can rotate, like an elbow.
terms.skinning: Linking the mesh's surface to the bones so it bends and stretches smoothly when the bones move.
terms.performance cost: How much work the computer has to do. More precise collisions cost more and can make the game slower.

watchOut: Using PreciseConvexDecomposition on every small decoration slows your game down. Use Box for small things players will not touch, like cups on a shelf.
Setting `TextureID` will not override a mesh that already has PBR textures. Remove or edit the SurfaceAppearance instead.
A mesh with Box or Hull collision may block doorways or holes that look open. Check with the Collision fidelity visualization before you blame the mesh.
The Asset Manager can bulk-import meshes, but not ones with rigging, skinning, animation, accessories or facial animation. Use the Importer for those.
